newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish yields, repo seen rising - survey.
newsitem.headline: Swedish yields, repo seen rising - survey.

text.p: Swedish debt yields are expected to rise in the short- and long-term and the Riksbank's key repo rate will probably be raised by 25 basis points in early 1998, a Reuters survey of analysts showed.
The repo rate, which is currently 4.10 percent, is expected to be 4.46 percent in one year, analysts said. The repo rate has been unchanged since December 17, 1996,
"We thought the Riksbank should have begun increasing the repo rate earlier but if they start later it will mean rises will be more dramatic," one said.
The analyst said the Riksbank, Sweden's central bank, would probably mark the start of a series of increases with a 25 basis point hike in March 1998.
Longer bond yields are expected to rise to 6.98 percent from today's level of 6.77 and in one year will be 7.53 percent, the survey of analysts showed.
The spread between longer Swedish and German yields is seen narrowing to 103 basis points from the present level of 107.
"The interest rate spread is expected to narrow because of increased confidence in Sweden due to improvements in state finances," one economist said.
"High yielding countries will see interest rates fall while German yields will increase in part because of economic trends and also because of increased convergence," the economist said.
Nordbanken economist Tomas Pousette said the spread between longer Swedish and German yields would fall to 80 basis points in one year and the Swedish ten-year bond yield would then be 7.20 percent.
"The yield spread will fall because state finances are better, the unemployment rate is going in the right direction and growth is improving," Pousette said.
Even if Swedish bond yields were to rise from current levels, German ones would increase still more, Pousette said.
"German bond yields will rise when the economy picks up a little," Pousette said.
However, other analysts said the spread between Swedish and German bond yields would rise because of domestic problems.
"The political situation (in Sweden) bothers me. There is a risk of a parliament without stable majorities and an expansionary budget ahead of the elections," said Unibank economist Bjorn Englund.
He forecast a spread of 125 basis points between German and Swedish long yields in three months' and 12 months' time.
Other analysts said high wage increases in Sweden were also a problem.
The crown was expected to strengthen to 4.43 against the mark within a year, to 4.46 in one month and 4.45 in three months.
